 What's happening now
 • Ground stop: Domestic US flights are being allowed to depart again after federal officials issued an hours-long ground stop due to safety concerns from a telecommunications outage . Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy blamed old air traffic control technology and overloaded routers.
 • Update problem: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pointed to FAA updates to those aging systems as the reason behind the halt. He added the ground stop did not stem from a threat to the US and was not linked to this week’s disruptive Microsoft outage.
 • Call to Congress: Duffy warned of more disruption unless the system is updated, repeatedly urging Congress to provide funds for improvements. It’s “going to be slow” to return to normal, he said , adding that it shouldn’t impact Thanksgiving travel in a couple weeks.
 • Travel nightmare: More than 7,700 flights within, into, or out of the US were canceled Friday and more than 8,000 were delayed, according to FlightAware . More than 2,000 such flights have been canceled for Saturday.

 Mom and toddler among passengers giving up on travel plans 
 1:19
 We’re now getting more on the adverse effects this disruption is having on air travelers around the country. Some passengers are giving up on their flight plans after hours of chaos and cancellations, CNN’s Julia Vargas Jones reported Friday night from Chicago O’Hare International Airport.
 Melissa Ogden was waiting to take off for San Francisco with her toddler when they were told to disembark the plane.
 Her daughter, perched on her hip back at the airport, looked up at her and summed up the forlorn situation: “All done.”
 Ogden told CNN: “We were delayed for a couple hours, and then we were on the plane for a couple hours. We waited a long time. And then we got back in here, back to square one… we all want it to be done.”
 She added: “We’re just glad that we weren’t in the air when it happened.”
 The mom, who had planned to visit the San Francisco Bay Area ahead of a work trip in the city, said she has decided not to rebook her flight.
 “There is no way, if they get all this stuff figured out, that a flight is going to go any time soon. Even after they figure it out, there is going to be a cascading effect so we were like ‘Let’s just go home.’
 “They told us our bags are going to go to San Francisco without us, that’s all we’ve been told.”
 Vargas Jones said many passengers are being told to try again tomorrow for their flights, with some admitting they want to give up.
 Another group, who had just met at a salesforce conference, told CNN they decided to abandon their flight altogether and rent a car to drive the 800 miles back to New York instead.

 Air traffic controllers 'don't buy' Duffy's explanation for FAA ground stop 
 2:04
 Some air traffic controllers “don’t buy” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy’s explanation for what prompted Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop order, according to a national security reporter for the Washington Examiner.
 Anna Giaritelli told CNN’s Laura Coates she had been in contact with 60 air traffic controllers and “none of them are buying what he said.”
 The nationwide ground stop was issued after air traffic control routers became overloaded with data and started to give inconsistent readings, Duffy said. The secretary blamed the issue on the country’s “incredibly old” air traffic control system. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the system failure as a result of patching new technology into an existing framework which caused the older system to get overwhelmed.
 But Giaritelli said “these types of switches they’re doing that the FAA is doing, they don’t happen during the day. They don’t happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They’re doing these midweek, middle of the night when there is no air traffic going on.”

 What to do if your flight is canceled or delayed by the FAA ground stop
 By Forrest Brown 
 People walk past a screen displaying information of delayed and cancelled flights after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop on Friday night. 
 Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters 
 Friday’s nationwide ground stop is a reminder that flights can get canceled and delayed at any time and for numerous reasons – from bad weather and mechanical issues to operational glitches.
 Keep in mind that in the United States, when an airline cancels your flight, you are entitled to a refund if you choose not to travel.
 “If a flight does get canceled, travelers are owed a full refund for the ticket, full stop. If they are presented with a credit, they have the right to refuse and ask for monetary refund,” said Katy Nastro, a spokesperson for travel site Going.com , who was underlining Department of Transportation rules .
 If a big storm or another complication seems poised to disrupt your flights, “look to make alternative travel plans immediately,” said Eric Napoli, chief legal officer at AirHelp , an air passenger rights company. Competition for seats becomes fierce during the holiday season when flights are more full.
 “Travelers should consider looking at flights that are very early in the morning — as these are typically less delayed, too,” Napoli said.
 Here’s more on what experts say you should do if your flight is delayed or canceled.

 More than 2,000 flights in the US canceled for Saturday
 By Helen Regan 
 Flight statuses change from delayed to cancelled at the San Diego International Airport after the FAA issued an emergency nationwide ground stoppage on Friday night. 
 Luke Johnson/The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty Images 
 Travelers can expect further flight disruptions tomorrow as US aviation recovers from Friday’s hours-long ground stop that halted air travel across the country.
 More than 2,000 flights within, into, or out of the US are canceled for Saturday, according to flight data tracker FlightAware. And more than 300 flights are expected to be delayed.
 Already more than 7,700 flights within, into, or out of the US were canceled today and more than 8,000 were delayed, according to FlightAware.
 Some planes began flying again Friday evening and major airlines said they are working to resume operations. But passengers have been told to expect disruptions into the weekend as airlines work to clear the backlog of planes and find crew to fly them.

 Changes to Saturday's college football schedule
 By Jacob Lev 
 Multiple college football games scheduled for Saturday – including three featuring top-25 teams - have been affected by the nationwide ground stop.
 One of the biggest games of the weekend which features No. 2 Utah on the road at No. 23 Arizona has been pushed back three hours, to 10:30 p.m. ET.
 No. 10 BYU is now set to host Baylor at 7 p.m. ET, moving back from an original 3:30 p.m. ET start.
 Mississippi State’s home game against Auburn has been moved from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. ET.
 The University of Central Florida’s home game against Arizona State is now scheduled to kick off at 5:30 p.m. ET after it was originally slated for 4:15 p.m. ET.
 Tulane will take on Rice at 4:30 p.m. ET instead of 2 p.m. ET, and Florida Atlantic will now play Tulsa at 7:15 p.m. ET. Kansas at West Virginia has moved up to 3:30 p.m. ET.

 Stranded passengers left with few good options following ground stop 
 1:34
 In testimony that underscores the stress and uncertainty facing thousands around the country, a passenger stranded at Miami International Airport has told CNN he’s hoping, at best, for a complimentary hotel stay – to avoid spending the night on the airport floor.
 The passenger arrived on a flight from El Salvador. His connecting flight was delayed by three hours, and then ultimately canceled.
 “There’s no more flights tonight, so I don’t know. I’m just trying to get a free hotel or something… I’m trying to make it home,” he told CNN’s Carolina Peguero at the Miami hub.
 When asked where he would sleep otherwise, he said: “Here in the airport, on the floor somewhere.”
 He added: “I got another trip planned on Tuesday, so I’m flying back to Orlando… I got stuff to do tomorrow so it’s complicated.”
 Other passengers have managed to rebook their flights, but not until tomorrow, while some are resorting to rental cars to continue their journey, Peguero said.

 Trump urges Congress to fast-track air traffic control overhaul in call with senator
 By Kit Maher 
 US President Donald Trump speaks at the White House in Washington, DC, on November 5. 
 Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters 
 President Donald Trump in a phone call tonight with GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt pushed for Congress to pass legislation modernizing air traffic control, airport towers, terminals and other critical infrastructure as soon as possible, said a source familiar with the conversation.
 Schmitt called the president before tonight’s briefing at the White House, the source said.
 Schmitt, who serves on the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, introduced the Modern Skies Act in September, which would provide $30 billion in additional federal funding to update the nation’s aviation infrastructure. He is pushing for it to be included in reconciliation so the funding can pass sooner.
 The Trump administration sent a letter to Congress this morning, hours before the ground stop, asking for the $30 billion in additional funding, the source said. The letter from director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was sent to leadership on the Senate Appropriations Committee.

 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pointed to FAA updates to the air traffic control system as the reason behind today’s nationwide ground stop. He said the FAA added new technology to the old system, causing the massive breakdown.
 “What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology… it was overwhelming the older system,” Mullin said.
 Mullin cited the failure of the patches as evidence that the FAA systems need a “complete overhaul.”

 The ground stop is over, but here's what we still don’t know
 By Helen Regan 
 A person takes a photo of a screen displaying information on delayed and cancelled flights at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Friday. 
 Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters 
 Federal officials have warned it will take time for airports and airlines to reach full capacity again following today’s hours-long ground stop that halted flights across the country and caused travel chaos for tens of thousands of people.
 Some flights are resuming, but many questions remain about what the weekend will look like for passengers and airlines, and how to prevent the disruption from happening again.
 Here’s what we know, and don’t know, about the hours and days ahead: 
 Why it happened: The nationwide ground stop was issued this afternoon after air traffic control routers became overloaded with data and started to give inconsistent readings, US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. The secretary blamed the issue on the country’s “incredibly old” air traffic control system. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the system failure as a result of patching new technology into an existing framework which caused the older system to get overwhelmed.
 Untangling the airspace mess: Some passengers are sitting on planes, waiting for hours on the tarmac as airports don’t have the gate space to allow them to disembark. Duffy warned it could take until tomorrow to move flights, as it depends on whether airports have space and whether pilots and crew are available. Large crowds and long queues of people could be seen at airports and baggage claims across the country Friday evening.
 Which airline flights remain canceled: Because of the congestion, some airlines have canceled flights tonight. JetBlue Airways has called off its remaining flights for Friday and said it expects disruptions to continue into Saturday. More than 1,600 flights within, into, or out of the US are canceled for Saturday, according to flight data tracker FlightAware. Meanwhile, Delta and United said they have resumed operations , but expect disruptions into the weekend. Airlines are asking passengers to check their latest flight status.
 What needs to be done: Transportation Secretary Duffy warned that more disruptions to air travel would happen unless the system is updated , and repeatedly urged Congress to act on legislation that would give them more money to improve the systems. Homeland Security Secretary Mullin called for a “complete overhaul” of FAA’s technology systems, which he said could cost about $50 billion.
 Read more

 Link Copied!
 Here's what major US airlines are saying after ground stop was lifted
 From CNN Staff
 Passengers queue at Delta airlines baggage service counter at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Friday. 
 Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters 
 After the ground stop was lifted following four hours of travel disruptions and thousands of flight cancellations and delays, some airlines said flights would resume while others said the impacts could drag into the weekend.
 Delta Air Lines has resumed all scheduled flights following the Federal Aviation Administration order lifting the nationwide ground stop. “Please visit the Delta app or check your flight status for more information,” the airline said on its website. The airline is offering flexibility options and the ability to adjust travel plans, it said. 
 United Airlines said it is resuming operations, including some Friday night flights. “Safety is our highest priority as we take care of our customers and employees,” the airline said. Customers who have received travel waivers can change their travel plans this weekend as disruptions are expected to continue on Saturday, the airline said. Customers can check the latest flight status at united.com or the United app.
 Southwest Airlines is resuming a limited number of flights, with schedules adjusted according to crew location and availability, it said Friday evening ET. The company has also issued a waiver allowing customers to cancel or rebook their flights at a later date without penalty.
 Frontier Airlines said it is “working to restore operations.” Travelers can check their flight status and emails for updates, the airline said.
 JetBlue Airways called off its remaining flights for Friday and said it expects disruptions to continue into Saturday.

 CNN’s Kristen Holmes asks why the agency wasn’t prepared for the type of catastrophic failure like today 
 1:58
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that more disruptions to air travel would happen unless the system is updated, repeatedly urging Congress to act on legislation that would give them more money to improve the systems.
 “You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said in response to a question from CNN’s Kristen Holmes.
 Holmes asked Duffy why the agency wasn’t prepared for the type of catastrophic failure like today.
 “Well, I can’t anticipate every catastrophic failure that’ll happen with a TDM network, with an analog network,” he replied.
 When another reporter asked Duffy to explain what he meant by this happening again, he said he didn’t know specifics.

 The SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy V3 Booster lift off from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, Friday afternoon. REUTERS/Steve Nesius

 Commercial space companies work closely with the Federal Aviation Administration: Before today’s launch could take place, SpaceX needed an FAA launch license, for example. And the agency issues NOTAMs — or Notice to Airmen — in order to clear air traffic around the launch site to ensure the rocket has a clear path for liftoff.
 But SpaceX does not rely on the same flight tracking infrastructure as aircraft. The company uses its own telemetry, gathered directly from Starship, to ensure the vehicle is operating as intended and on the correct flight path.
 Infrastructure from the US Space Force is also the primary means of tracking traffic in Earth orbit.

 FAA lifts ground stop but delays and cancellations persist. Here's what we know
 By Helen Regan 
 People sit on the floor as they wait to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Friday, in the Queens borough of New York. 
 Adam Gray/Getty Images 
 More than four hours after all US flight departures were halted, causing travel chaos across the country, the Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday evening.
 But frustrated travelers will continue to face delayed or canceled flights and hours-long waits at airports, as federal officials warned it will take time for airports and airlines to get back to full capacity.
 Here’s what we know and don’t know: 
 • Why were planes grounded? The FAA announced a ground stop for all flights in the US this afternoon. A ground stop requires aircraft to remain on the ground and bars them from taking off, and more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when it was issued.
 • What caused the issue? US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said old air traffic control technology and routers overloaded with data were to blame for the nationwide ground stop today. Earlier, the FAA told airlines the problem is believed to have started at Chicago Midway International Airport and cascaded nationwide.
 • Not a cyberattack: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his department has seen “ zero evidence ” that the telecommunications issue causing the ground stop was a cyberattack. But he said they were still investigating, “so we’re not going to rule that out.”
 • What has been the impact? While Mullin stressed the public was not in danger, thousands of passengers across the country faced a travel nightmare. About 15,000 flights have either been delayed or canceled today, and more than 700 flights within, into, or out of the US are canceled for Saturday, according to flight data tracker FlightAware. Airports are continuing to tell passengers to confirm their flight status with their airline before going to the airport. Many travelers are now deciding whether to keep waiting it out or make other plans. Passengers deboarding one plane told CNN they were sitting on a tarmac for more than an hour and a half.
 • Airports running out of space: With so many aircraft unable to fly because of the nationwide ground stop, airports were running out of gates and tarmac space to park planes. An airport source said the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport does not have any more space to park planes and can no longer accept diversions.
 • International disruptions: Eurocontrol, Europe’s air traffic control authority, suspended all US-bound departures from its 42 member countries on Friday at the FAA’s request. The suspension was scheduled to run until midnight ET. US-bound flights from major airports in Asia were also affected by the disruption.
